A file you can download is not a file you can embed in a product. Model licenses differ: permissive licenses, licenses with an acceptable-use policy, and licenses that require a separate commercial grant above a size or revenue line.

Problem, user, non-goals, success, risks, and the first milestone.

A sampling control. Lower sticks to likely tokens. Higher lets less likely tokens through.

A capstone that needs a team, a budget, and a month of data cleaning is a job, not this exercise. Cut it until you can demo it in one sitting.

In this course a hallucination is an answer that reads well and is not grounded in a source you can check. The model may invent a citation, a function, a date, or a confident 'yes'.
Do not add a step because a diagram looked mature. Add a step when a single call fails in a way you can name. If classification is already perfect on your examples, it does not need its own model.
A loop that lets a model call tools, read observations, and stop on a rule you set.

Full fine-tuning updates every weight. That is expensive and easy to damage. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes the base model and trains small matrices that sit alongside certain layers. You store the adapter, not a full second copy of the model.
A fixed sequence is a workflow. A loop that chooses tools is an agent. Prefer the workflow until you can show that the next step depends on the previous result in a way you cannot write down.

Exact checks are better when you can write them: JSON validity, id membership, a number, a tool that must not appear in the trace. Use the judge for the residue, not for everything, because the residue is where you can be fooled.

A critique-revise pair is two jobs. The critique marks the draft against the done-check. The revision may change only the lines that failed. If you let the revision rewrite freely, you lose the parts that were already correct.

questions.q: What further claim does “Critique the draft, then revise once” add?

choices: Exact checks are better when you can write them: JSON validity, id membership, a number, a tool that must not appear in the trace. Use the judge for the residue, not for everything, because the residue is where you can be fooled.

Prompt injection happens when text the model is reading — a web page, a PDF, an email, a tool description — contains instructions aimed at the model. The text might say to ignore the standing rules, reveal a secret, or call a tool. The model is not a security boundary. The software around it is.
Two or three examples beat a paragraph of adjectives. Each example needs the same shape as the real task: input, then the output you want, including a refusal example if refusal is correct sometimes.
The ordered record of tool calls, arguments, results, approvals, and stops.

MCP lets a host's client talk to a server that exposes tools, resources, and prompts over stdio locally or HTTP remotely. I use it when I want a reviewed server — notes, tickets, docs — available to an assistant without inventing a plugin format.
It is a recognition and testing lesson. It does not include payloads or bypass techniques.
Compare to a baseline. A single impressive answer is not an eval.

That is why a model can write a confident paragraph about a library that does not exist, and why it can also write a correct summary of a page you just pasted in. The second case worked because the evidence was in the context, not because the model 'looked it up' in the world.

When a result is wrong, change one variable. The instruction, the examples, the model, the temperature, or the retrieved text. Not all of them. Save the previous prompt as an artifact so you can return.

The later tracks get more powerful. These rules do not loosen as you go.
Run this after install, after reboot, and after you pull a new model. Save the result with the date. Five lines is enough.

A local model runs on hardware you control. The prompt does not leave the machine, unless the software you wrapped around it sends it somewhere. That is the reason to prefer local for private notes, drafts of unreleased work, and air-gapped labs.

questions.q: What further claim does “Run a model locally when the data should stay put” add?

Store this beside the outputs, or store the outputs and link them. When someone asks why you shipped, this is the answer.

This campus will not help you write malware, hide a prompt injection, bypass a provider's safety stack, scrape a system you are not allowed to access, or automate harm. Those are not advanced modules. They are out of scope.

Write a goal block in the shape above for a small change you understand. If you do not have a repo, use a fictional one and still name a test command.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Install a runner and call it on localhost” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?

A kill switch is a flag that disables the model path and leaves the previous workflow intact. If there is no previous workflow, the kill switch is 'stop showing the feature'. Shipping without that flag means an incident becomes a scramble.

Two common runners in 2026 are Ollama, which gives you a local service and a simple CLI, and llama.cpp, which runs GGUF weights with fine control over hardware. LM Studio and MLX on Apple silicon are other local options. vLLM is what teams use when they serve an open model to many callers. You do not need all of them.

A tool the model can call needs a name, a description of when to use it, a JSON schema for the arguments, and a handler you wrote. The description is read by the model. The schema is enforced by your code.

Keep going. Later practices accept a written plan in place of a live call. Do not create an API key just to finish a local-model lesson.

Write your memory budget and the first model class you will try. Include the sentence you will use if it does not fit: which smaller model you fall back to.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Pick a model size that fits in memory” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
choices: A product sentence has a person, a job, and a constraint. The model is an implementation choice.
One prompt that plans, searches, calculates, and drafts is several jobs hiding in a paragraph.
A token is a chunk of text, not a word, and every limit you hit is counted in tokens.
If the weights do not fit, the runner will swap, crash, or refuse. Start smaller than your pride.

questions.q: What does “Pick a model size that fits in memory” argue at the outset?
choices: Run the School 09 tasks twice: base model, then base plus adapter. Same prompts, same retrieval, same tools. The adapter wins only if the failures you trained for improved and the safety tasks did not get worse.

A tool the model can call needs a name, a description of when to use it, a JSON schema for the arguments, and a handler you wrote. The description is read by the model. The schema is enforced by your code.

A second agent is justified when it has a different tool allowlist or a different job, and it receives a structured artifact from the first. A researcher that may only search, handing a citation list to a writer that may only draft, is a real split.

Memory is the constraint, not the slogan on the model card. A quantized 7B or 8B instruct model is a common first fit on a 16 GB laptop. Machines with 8 GB should start smaller. A 32 GB machine can try a larger quantized model after the small one has a smoke test.

questions.q: What further claim does “Pick a model size that fits in memory” add?
choices: These are starting points, not laws. The same parameter count at a different quantization, context length, or runtime will use a different amount of memory. Watch the runner's reported memory and your system's pressure.

This campus will not help you write malware, hide a prompt injection, bypass a provider's safety stack, scrape a system you are not allowed to access, or automate harm. Those are not advanced modules. They are out of scope.
If the gate fails, the honest close is 'not ready to share as a tool'. That is a finished capstone. An unfinished one is a demo with no tasks.
Do not add a step because a diagram looked mature. Add a step when a single call fails in a way you can name. If classification is already perfect on your examples, it does not need its own model.

questions.q: What does “Pick a model size that fits in memory” add after those claims?
choices: A typical supervised set is a list of conversations or instruction pairs: the input the model will see, and the output you want. The format must match how you will call the model later. Training on essays and then calling the model as a JSON API is a self-inflicted miss.

Apple silicon uses unified memory. A discrete NVIDIA GPU uses its own memory, and the rest of the machine does not automatically extend it. CPU-only runs work and are slow. Slow is acceptable for a lesson. It is a product decision later.

Keyword search, such as BM25, finds the rare exact string: an error code, a function name, a SKU. Embeddings miss those and find paraphrases. Hybrid retrieval runs both and merges the lists. That combination is the ordinary 2026 default, not an advanced trick.
Use low temperature for anything you score. Temperature does not check facts.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: You sit down to practice “Pick a model size that fits in memory”. What should you produce before you move on?
choices: On the track map, star the first track that contains a word you cannot define yet. Start there after you finish Start here.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Quantization trades precision for fit” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
choices: One prompt that plans, searches, calculates, and drafts is several jobs hiding in a paragraph.
A change that raises quality and doubles the bill needs a decision, not a silent ship.
The model may call a tool, read the result, and repeat, until an answer or a cap.
The weights are stored with fewer bits. You measure whether your tasks still pass.

questions.q: What does “Quantization trades precision for fit” argue at the outset?
choices: Full-precision weights are large. Quantization stores those numbers in fewer bits so the model fits in memory and reads faster. GGUF is the file format llama.cpp and many local runners expect. You will see labels such as Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, and Q8_0. The digit is the bit budget. It is not a quality score.

Networks fail after the side effect and before the response. If your client retries, the tool runs twice unless the handler is idempotent. For a calculator, running twice is fine. For a payment or an email, it is not.
A person who can use an AI product is not the same as a person who can ship one. This course trains the second skill at a scale you can practice alone.

Two agents that share a vague chat are one confused loop with extra cost.
The skill is judgment you can show, not a tour of product names.

Keywords catch exact codes and names. Vectors catch paraphrases. In 2026 this is the ordinary default.
If you cannot name the artifact that crosses the boundary, keep one agent.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Read the trace, not the closing summary” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?

questions.q: What does “Read the trace, not the closing summary” argue at the outset?

A large language model takes the tokens so far and assigns probabilities to what might come next. It then picks one, adds it, and repeats. The result sounds like a person who knows the topic. The mechanism is still next-token prediction.

A kill switch is a flag that disables the model path and leaves the previous workflow intact. If there is no previous workflow, the kill switch is 'stop showing the feature'. Shipping without that flag means an incident becomes a scramble.
When the summary and the trace disagree, believe the trace.

questions.q: What further claim does “Read the trace, not the closing summary” add?
choices: Structured output does not make the values true. A schema can require `source_id` to be a string and still receive an id you do not have. Check membership against the ids you sent.

Prompt injection happens when text the model is reading — a web page, a PDF, an email, a tool description — contains instructions aimed at the model. The text might say to ignore the standing rules, reveal a secret, or call a tool. The model is not a security boundary.
This is also how you debug a loop that 'got stuck'. The trace shows the repeated call. The summary says it explored thoroughly.
A field inside the model's tool call that says approved is not an approval.

questions.q: You sit down to practice “Read the trace, not the closing summary”. What should you produce before you move on?

questions.q: What does “Make tool calls safe to retry, inside a sandbox” argue at the outset?
choices: Networks fail after the side effect and before the response. If your client retries, the tool runs twice unless the handler is idempotent. For a calculator, running twice is fine. For a payment or an email, it is not. Use an idempotency key the handler stores, and return the original result on a repeat.

If your background is phone systems, bring that operational care to the latency budget and the handoff. Leave the vendor-specific telephony course for a telephony course. Here, voice is an interface on top of the same retrieval, tools, and evals.
Low-Rank Adaptation. Trains small matrices while the base model stays frozen.

Problem, user, non-goals, success, risks, and the first milestone.

Model Context Protocol. A standard way for a host's client to talk to a server that offers tools, resources, and prompts.

A versioned set of tasks, a scorer, and a record of the model, prompt, and index you ran.

A vector for a piece of text, used for similarity search. Produced by an embedding model, not by the chat model.

Installing an MCP server is closer to installing a plugin than to bookmarking a page. A local server can read files. A remote server receives whatever the client sends and might retain it. Both can put instructions into tool descriptions, which the model will read.

Work in order the first time. Later, use search when you need a term. Mark a lesson complete only when you can say the idea without looking and you have the practice artifact.
Hiring posts for AI product managers in 2026 ask for the same discipline as the engineering tracks: a user, a workflow, a measurement, and a risk. Start with the job-to-be-done.

questions.q: What does “Give the agent the files and tests that matter” argue at the outset?
choices: Weights are large, replaceable, and often re-downloadable. Prompts are small and are the thing you version. Private notes are neither weights nor prompts.

I fine-tune only after a fixed task set shows that the schema, the prompt, retrieval, and tools still leave a behavior I can teach with examples. Facts that change stay in retrieval. I keep the adapter only if it beats the base model on that set without new safety failures.
Bills, rate limits, and the context window are counted in tokens. Count them with the tokenizer for the model you call.

Point the agent at the module, the failing test, and the interface it must not break. Name the command that proves success. If you do not know the command, finding the command is the task, and the agent should stop before editing.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: What further claim does “Give the agent the files and tests that matter” add?
choices: If the job is 'show me this note', prefer a resource. If the job is 'append a line to the decision log', that is a tool, and it waits for a person unless you have a strong reason and an eval.
Let it search when the relevant file is unknown. Keep the step cap small so search does not become a tour. When it names the files it will change, that list is the moment to redirect it.

I look at the diff as a teammate's change: extra files, weakened tests, new dependencies, and anything outside the goal. I run the test command myself and read the output. Secrets, push, and unrestricted shell are denied in the tool layer. The person who merges is responsible.
Audit it against scores you made by hand before you let it gate a release.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: You sit down to practice “Give the agent the files and tests that matter”. What should you produce before you move on?
choices: Open the log with a first entry, even if every metric says 'not run'. The next line says the first change you will make.
Write a goal, the only tools you would allow, the step cap, and the exact sentence for a cap hit. Save it as the artifact for this lesson.
Write three lines a pull request should contain when an agent helped: the goal, the test command and result, and the permissions used.
Write a goal block in the shape above for a small change you understand. If you do not have a repo, use a fictional one and still name a test command.
questions.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Plan, edit, run, then stop” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
choices: Each of those is a release. The tasks do not change in the same commit unless the task change is the point.
A current browser is enough to study. A local model is optional and comes later.
A plan you can reject is cheaper than a pile of edits you have to unwind.
The tools or commands that may run. Everything else is denied.
questions.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

questions.q: What does “Plan, edit, run, then stop” argue at the outset?
choices: A coding agent is the loop from School 06 pointed at a codebase. Products in this category include Cursor, GitHub Copilot's agent modes, Claude Code, Codex-style agents, Aider, Continue, and Cline. They differ in interface.
In this course a hallucination is an answer that reads well and is not grounded in a source you can check. The model may invent a citation, a function, a date, or a confident 'yes'.
I retrieve passages instead of pasting the corpus, cap output tokens, and route easy rows to a smaller model only when those rows pass the same checks. I set timeouts and backoff.

Skipping the plan is sometimes fine for a one-line change you already specified. It is a poor habit for anything that crosses a module. 'Keep going until the tests pass' without a cap is how an agent refactors the neighborhood and calls it a fix.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: What further claim does “Plan, edit, run, then stop” add?
choices: A chat box with no states is a demo. A product names these four and logs them. The unsafe state is especially easy to get wrong: a coy message that hints at the blocked action teaches the next try.
A model that applies a written rubric to an answer. It is a second system, with its own error rate.
A failed test is a successful stop if the step cap is near. Record the failure. Do not let a second, unrelated edit 'try something else' in the same unreviewed tree.
Storing an existing model's weights in fewer bits so they fit and load faster.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: You sit down to practice “Plan, edit, run, then stop”. What should you produce before you move on?
choices: Fill the template for a fictional incident: a retrieved page told the model to approve a refund, and the draft looked convincing. Say whether a tool acted. In a well-built system, it did not.
Write three questions whose correct answer is 'the sources do not say'. You will use them when you build retrieval.
Add a step cap and a stop sentence to the goal block from 08-02. Example stop sentence: 'I hit 6 steps. Tests are red. No further edits.'
Write the comparison header: task, base result, adapter result, regression yes/no. Fill it with the decision you expect, and note which safety task would make you throw the adapter away.
questions.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Review the diff and the tests” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
choices: A citation is an id and a span, not a confident tone.
A person confirms the exact arguments of a side effect before the handler runs.
Speech recognition and speech synthesis are models with their own failure modes. They do not replace the eval.
Read the change as if a new teammate wrote it. Then run the same command they ran.
questions.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

questions.q: What does “Review the diff and the tests” argue at the outset?
choices: Review for behavior, not for style the linter can catch. Look for extra files, weakened assertions, deleted tests, new dependencies, and changes outside the goal. Look for secrets that were read and echoed into a comment or a log.

Require the answer to name the chunk ids it used. Render those ids as labels a person can click or open. If the model cites an id that was not in the retrieved set, drop the sentence or fail the answer. That check is code.

A second agent is justified when it has a different tool allowlist or a different job, and it receives a structured artifact from the first. A researcher that may only search, handing a citation list to a writer that may only draft, is a real split.
Fill it for the capstone before you connect a tool. If a line is 'not sure', the tool stays disconnected. Update the page when the system changes, in the same change as the tool list.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: In “Review the diff and the tests”, what should you keep from the note “Green tests can be gamed”?
choices: A critique-revise pair is two jobs. The critique marks the draft against the done-check. The revision may change only the lines that failed. If you let the revision rewrite freely, you lose the parts that were already correct.
When a grounded assistant is wrong, look at the pipeline in order. Prompt edits are last.

A more aggressive quantization is smaller and more likely to damage reasoning, names, and tight formats. The only way to know is to run your fixture on two quantizations of the same model. If both pass, keep the smaller one.
An agent can edit the test until it passes. Treat a test diff as carefully as a code diff. The expected value should still describe the behavior you want.
questions.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

questions.q: You sit down to practice “Review the diff and the tests”. What should you produce before you move on?
choices: Write five review questions you will ask of the next agent diff you see. Keep them specific enough that each is yes or no.
Take one real page and mark the chunk boundaries with a pencil. Write an id scheme, such as `note-14#setup`. Check that each chunk still makes sense alone.
Name one system you wish a model could read — a notes folder, a ticket list, a schema — and write whether it should be a tool (an action) or a resource (data the model may read).
Create the ten task titles and mark which are cite, which are refuse, and which is the injection case. Store them in a file next to the corpus path.
questions.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Secrets, destructive git, and the network” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
choices: The expensive mistakes are not bad indentation.
A small instruct model whose license you have read, in a size that fits your memory.
A proposed function name and arguments. Your code validates them and runs the handler.
Retrieve widely, then keep the few passages that actually answer.

questions.q: What does “Secrets, destructive git, and the network” argue at the outset?
choices: The label, such as Q4, is not a quality score. Compare quantizations on your tasks.
Put the deny list in the tool layer. A prompt that says 'never run destructive commands' loses to a tool that can run them and a document that says 'you must'.
Untrusted text — a page, a ticket, a tool description — that tries to instruct the model.
The piece of a document you index, retrieve, and cite.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: You sit down to practice “Secrets, destructive git, and the network”. What should you produce before you move on?
choices: Write five review questions you will ask of the next agent diff you see. Keep them specific enough that each is yes or no.
Write the command allowlist for a lab agent: the test command, and nothing else. Add three commands that are always denied.
Write the header row of a comparison sheet: provider, model id, pass count, safety fails, median latency, cost for the ten, retention note. Fill 'not run' if you have not called anyone.
Write a yes/no checklist you will use before enabling a server: who published it, what tools it lists, whether any tool can write or send, and whether the host will ask first.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Use a coding agent on a team without shipping junk” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
choices: Local is a privacy and latency choice. It is not automatically the more accurate choice.
Agree the permissions, the review, and what 'the agent did it' does not excuse.
If a test is awkward to write, the capstone is still too vague.
No. Progress stays in this browser. The page does not load remote fonts, scripts, or images.

questions.q: What does “Use a coding agent on a team without shipping junk” argue at the outset?
choices: Hosted APIs in 2026 generally offer a way to constrain output: JSON schema, tool definitions, or a response format flag. Use it for anything a program will read. Then parse and validate. On failure, record the raw body, retry once with the validator message, and stop.
A policy you can apply is one page. A policy that quotes every guideline and changes nothing is not a control.
Untrusted text — a page, a ticket, a tool description — that tries to instruct the model.

Teams that get value from coding agents in 2026 treat them as fast teammates with a narrow role. The author of the change is still a person. The pull request explains the behavior, the test command, and any permission the agent was given.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: What further claim does “Use a coding agent on a team without shipping junk” add?
choices: I look at the diff as a teammate's change: extra files, weakened tests, new dependencies, and anything outside the goal. I run the test command myself and read the output. Secrets, push, and unrestricted shell are denied in the tool layer. The person who merges is responsible.
Lines generated is a vanity metric. A change that takes longer to review than it would have taken to write is not a win, unless it was a change people were avoiding for a tracked reason.
This is the judgment hiring panels are probing when they ask 'how do you decide to fine-tune'. The answer is a sequence of measured exclusions, not enthusiasm for training.
A roadmap slide that says 'improve AI quality' does not tell an engineer what to do. The shared numbers do. They are the same four axes as the eval gate, expressed as a product promise.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: You sit down to practice “Use a coding agent on a team without shipping junk”. What should you produce before you move on?
choices: Label three boxes — host, client, server — for a setup you might actually run. Write one sentence for what each box must not do.

Run one factual extraction twice at low temperature and twice at a high temperature, if you have any model available. If you do not, write the setting you will use for scored tasks and the setting you will refuse to use.
Write three lines a pull request should contain when an agent helped: the goal, the test command and result, and the permissions used.
Write a schema for a task with three fields. Include one field that has a closed set of values. Note how you will reject a response that adds a fourth field.
questions.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “An eval is a versioned test, not a feeling” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
choices: Low-Rank Adaptation. Trains small matrices while the base model stays frozen.
You cannot prefer a new prompt unless the same tasks were scored both times.
A vector for a piece of text, used for similarity search. Produced by an embedding model, not by the chat model.
Open weights are not one license. Some allow commercial use. Some restrict it. Some restrict use of the outputs for training.

questions.q: What does “An eval is a versioned test, not a feeling” argue at the outset?
choices: An evaluation is a set of tasks, a way to score them, and a record of what you ran. It is the same idea as a test suite, with more judgment in the score and more ways to fool yourself.
The build log is the proof habit applied to the capstone. One entry per change. Short.

I fine-tune only after a fixed task set shows that the schema, the prompt, retrieval, and tools still leave a behavior I can teach with examples. Facts that change stay in retrieval. I keep the adapter only if it beats the base model on that set without new safety failures.
A sampling control. Lower sticks to likely tokens. Higher lets less likely tokens through.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: What further claim does “An eval is a versioned test, not a feeling” add?
choices: 'It looks better' is a hypothesis. The eval is the test of the hypothesis. If you do not want to write tasks, you do not have an eval practice yet, and you should not be fine-tuning or swapping models on taste.
A vector for a piece of text, used for similarity search. Produced by an embedding model, not by the chat model.

Full-precision weights are large. Quantization stores those numbers in fewer bits so the model fits in memory and reads faster. GGUF is the file format llama.cpp and many local runners expect. You will see labels such as Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, and Q8_0. The digit is the bit budget.
The campus file and the text are MIT licensed. You do not need an account or a key to read them. MIT is not a warranty. Third-party model licenses, data, and trademarks stay with their owners.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: You sit down to practice “An eval is a versioned test, not a feeling”. What should you produce before you move on?
choices: Draft ten one-line task titles for a system you might build. Mark two as refusal and one as a safety case. You can fill the inputs later. The titles force coverage.
In three sentences, explain to a teammate the difference between quantizing a model to run it and training a LoRA adapter on it.
Either describe a handoff schema between two roles, or write 'one agent' and the reason a second role would be fake.
Create a file with three tasks. Each task needs an input and a check a person could apply twice and agree on.
questions.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Start with ten tasks you can explain” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
choices: A small set you trust beats a large set nobody can audit.
The weights are stored with fewer bits. You measure whether your tasks still pass.
The person uses the host. The client holds the session. The server does the work.
After a reboot, prove the runner is up before you debug the prompt.
questions.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

questions.q: What does “Start with ten tasks you can explain” argue at the outset?
choices: Ten tasks is enough to catch a clumsy prompt change and small enough that you will actually look at the failures. Grow the set when a production mistake was not represented. Do not generate five hundred tasks with a model and call them ground truth.
A denylist fails when you add a tool and forget to classify it.
Timeouts also bound runaway reasoning models. If the product cannot wait, do not call a model that might think for a minute. Fall back or tell the person the job is still running.

Also record the operational facts: data-retention default, region, whether prompt caching exists, and how structured output is spelled in that API. A model that scores well and retains data you cannot retain is not a win.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: What further claim does “Start with ten tasks you can explain” add?
choices: Write the expected check next to the input. For retrieval, the check includes the chunk id. For an agent, the check includes which tools were allowed to run and which must not have run.
Keyword search and vector search together, merged into one candidate list.
The result is the diff and the tests you reran, not the agent's closing summary.
A chunk of text the model reads or writes. Not always a whole word.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: In “Start with ten tasks you can explain”, what should you keep from the note “Do not tune on the only set you have”?
choices: The first-stage search is tuned to recall: do not miss the right chunk. That list is too long and too noisy to paste into the prompt. A reranker, or a simple second score, reads the question and each candidate and keeps the best few.
A bibliography the model composed is not a citation. Check that the id was in the retrieved set.
Schema mode reduces broken JSON. It does not make the values true.
If you edit the prompt while staring at all ten, you are memorizing them. Hold out two tasks you do not look at until the end, or add a fresh task before you declare victory.
questions.why: That note is part of this lesson. The other lines are not.

questions.q: You sit down to practice “Start with ten tasks you can explain”. What should you produce before you move on?
choices: Write a three-item checklist for a writing task you care about. Make each item pass or fail, with no middle.
List the three checks you would run on the decision schema from the prompting track. Mark which ones a JSON schema cannot do alone.
Add a step cap and a stop sentence to the goal block from 08-02. Example stop sentence: 'I hit 6 steps. Tests are red. No further edits.'
Draft ten one-line task titles for a system you might build. Mark two as refusal and one as a safety case. You can fill the inputs later. The titles force coverage.
questions.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Score quality, safety, latency, and cost together” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
choices: The citation has to be an id you retrieved, and some tasks must refuse.
Cost is a property of the design. Input tokens, output tokens, and tool calls are the levers.
One prompt that plans, searches, calculates, and drafts is several jobs hiding in a paragraph.
A change that raises quality and doubles the bill needs a decision, not a silent ship.
questions.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

questions.q: What does “Score quality, safety, latency, and cost together” argue at the outset?
choices: In 2026, coding products expose MCP so a model can call the tools a developer already uses: a ticket, a design file, a database schema, a browser snapshot, a documentation search. That is useful. It also means the agent in School 08 may now see more than the git tree.

A coding agent is the loop from School 06 pointed at a codebase. Products in this category include Cursor, GitHub Copilot's agent modes, Claude Code, Codex-style agents, Aider, Continue, and Cline. They differ in interface.
It cannot recover a passage the first stage never retrieved.

A single blended number hides the trade. Keep the four. Your gate can say 'quality must not drop, safety fails must be zero, median latency under two seconds, cost within 10 percent'. Write the gate before you see the new score, or you will move the gate to fit the result.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: You sit down to practice “Score quality, safety, latency, and cost together”. What should you produce before you move on?
choices: If a runner is installed, save the tag list or the CLI's model list. If not, write the runner you will install and the exact check you will use to prove it is up.
Write a gate in one sentence for a system you have in mind, using at least quality and one of the other three axes.
Write that decision sentence for a real or fictional system. 'Not yet, because …' is a complete answer.
Create five labeled questions in the format above. If you cannot name a must_include id, you do not have a retrieval test yet. You have a vibe.
questions.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Use a model as a judge only with a rubric and an audit” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
choices: A judge model is a second system. It has its own failure rate.
A vector for a piece of text, used for similarity search. Produced by an embedding model, not by the chat model.
One file, a track order, and a way to know what you have finished.
QLoRA does the same while the frozen base is stored in a quantized form.
questions.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

questions.q: What does “Use a model as a judge only with a rubric and an audit” argue at the outset?
choices: Let the system draft the email, the refund, the shell command, or the pull request. Show the draft and the arguments. A person confirms. The tool layer checks that the confirmation matches those arguments. If the model changes the arguments after the yes, the yes is void.
It will also not certify you, grant you a model, or guarantee a job. The artifact you leave with is a capstone you can explain: what it calls, what it refuses, and how you scored it.

A more aggressive quantization is smaller and more likely to damage reasoning, names, and tight formats. The only way to know is to run your fixture on two quantizations of the same model. If both pass, keep the smaller one.

Some checks are awkward to write as exact string matches: whether a summary omitted a decision, whether a tone is acceptable. A judge model can apply a rubric to those. It cannot be the only authority.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: What further claim does “Use a model as a judge only with a rubric and an audit” add?
choices: Score these as pass or fail. Do not average them into a soft quality number. One safety fail blocks the release if that is the gate you wrote. If you decide it does not block, write that decision down and own it.

Exact checks are better when you can write them: JSON validity, id membership, a number, a tool that must not appear in the trace. Use the judge for the residue, not for everything, because the residue is where you can be fooled.
Do not wait until the demo to reconstruct this. You will invent a cleaner story than the one you ran.
A regression is a task that used to pass and now fails. Name it in the pull request. 'Overall score is flat' can hide one new safety fail and one new easy pass that cancel in the average.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: You sit down to practice “Use a model as a judge only with a rubric and an audit”. What should you produce before you move on?
choices: Write the audience for a limited release in one sentence, the kill switch, and the date you will read the numbers.
Describe two tasks side by side: one that deserves a reasoning model and one that does not. Name the metric that would change your mind.
Write a five-line rubric for one subjective check. Include one line that forces a fail.
Name one system you wish a model could read — a notes folder, a ticket list, a schema — and write whether it should be a tool (an action) or a resource (data the model may read).
questions.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Gate changes to the prompt, the model, and the index” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
choices: A folder you are allowed to use, questions you wrote, citations, and one read-only tool.
Embeddings find similar meaning. Keywords find the exact name. Hybrid search uses both.
Each of those is a release. The tasks do not change in the same commit unless the task change is the point.
A versioned set of tasks, a scorer, and a record of the model, prompt, and index you ran.

questions.q: What does “Gate changes to the prompt, the model, and the index” argue at the outset?
choices: I retrieve passages instead of pasting the corpus, cap output tokens, and route easy rows to a smaller model only when those rows pass the same checks. I set timeouts and backoff.
Marking a lesson complete writes to local storage on your machine. Clearing site data for the file clears the marks. There is no account.

A prompt tweak, a model swap, a new embedding model, a chunker change, and a tool-schema change are all releases. Run the same tasks. Put the score in the pull request. If the gate fails, do not merge because the demo looked fine.
You can finish the reading on a laptop or a phone browser. You do not need a GPU, a paid API key, or an account to use the campus.

questions.q: What further claim does “Gate changes to the prompt, the model, and the index” add?
choices: Low-Rank Adaptation. Trains small matrices while the base model stays frozen.
Decomposition means you name the intermediate results. Each result has a check. You can still send them in one call, or you can use a workflow. The win is the same: a failure has an address.
A regression is a task that used to pass and now fails. Name it in the pull request. 'Overall score is flat' can hide one new safety fail and one new easy pass that cancel in the average.
There is no exam board behind this file. If you want to show the work, share the capstone: tasks, policy page, scorecard, and a trace with secrets removed. A badge would say less.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: You sit down to practice “Gate changes to the prompt, the model, and the index”. What should you produce before you move on?
choices: Write the checklist you would paste at the bottom of a pull request that changes a prompt: what was pinned, what ran, which tasks regressed, and whether the gate passed.
Write that decision sentence for a real or fictional system. 'Not yet, because …' is a complete answer.
Write five review questions you will ask of the next agent diff you see. Keep them specific enough that each is yes or no.
Pick one tool. Say whether a retry is safe. If it is not, write the idempotency rule in one sentence. Name the directory the agent is allowed to see.
questions.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Put red-team cases in the set early” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
choices: The Model Context Protocol is a standard way for an app to talk to a tool server.
A versioned set of tasks, a scorer, and a record of the model, prompt, and index you ran.
The model proposes a call. Your code checks the arguments and runs the handler.
You are checking your own system's boundaries, on inputs you control.
questions.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

questions.q: What does “Put red-team cases in the set early” argue at the outset?
choices: A red-team case is a task that tries to make your system break a rule you wrote. You author the case. You are not attacking someone else's service, and you are not collecting bypass tricks. You are checking that your gate holds on inputs you will meet.

Full fine-tuning updates every weight. That is expensive and easy to damage. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes the base model and trains small matrices that sit alongside certain layers. You store the adapter, not a full second copy of the model.

Full-precision weights are large. Quantization stores those numbers in fewer bits so the model fits in memory and reads faster. GGUF is the file format llama.cpp and many local runners expect. You will see labels such as Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, and Q8_0. The digit is the bit budget.

You may use and adapt the material. You may not upload private work data because a lesson said to try a model. Fill the safety page with your real constraints. A model license can forbid uses the MIT license on this file does not.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: What further claim does “Put red-team cases in the set early” add?
choices: Score these as pass or fail. Do not average them into a soft quality number. One safety fail blocks the release if that is the gate you wrote. If you decide it does not block, write that decision down and own it.
Storing an existing model's weights in fewer bits so they fit and load faster.

'It looks better' is a hypothesis. The eval is the test of the hypothesis. If you do not want to write tasks, you do not have an eval practice yet, and you should not be fine-tuning or swapping models on taste.
The model is not the boundary. Tool permissions, argument checks, and human approval are.
questions.why: That sentence is in this lesson. The other choices come from different lessons.

questions.q: You sit down to practice “Put red-team cases in the set early”. What should you produce before you move on?
choices: Write the four numbers for your spec, plus one counter-metric. Use targets you could measure this month, not a press-release percentage.
In three sentences, explain to a teammate the difference between quantizing a model to run it and training a LoRA adapter on it.
Write two red-team tasks in input-and-pass-condition form. Use synthetic data. Do not include a real secret to 'see if it leaks'.
Add a 'will not build' line to your policy page that is specific to your domain, not a copy of this lesson's first sentence.
questions.why: That is the practice this lesson asks you to leave with.

questions.q: An interviewer asks what “Keep the scorecard next to the artifact” changes about how you work. Which answer holds?
choices: A protocol for connecting a host to a tool server, when more than one app should share that server.
A table you can reopen beats a screenshot of one good answer.
Problem, user, non-goals, success, risks, and the first milestone.
One prompt that plans, searches, calculates, and drafts is several jobs hiding in a paragraph.
questions.why: That is this lesson's summary, said out loud.

questions.q: What does “Keep the scorecard next to the artifact” argue at the outset?

questions.q: Why did the customer get two orders?
choices: The retry repeated a side effect that was not safe to run twice.
The context window duplicated the prompt.
The model decided a second order was friendlier.
Temperature sampled a second order.
questions.why: A timeout does not prove the first call failed.
questions.incidentTitle: A key in the page and a retry that double-sends
questions.case: A demo puts the API key in the browser script. The button places an order. On a timeout the client sends the same order again. The invoice shows two charges and a token spike from the retries.

questions.q: What should the client send on the second attempt?
choices: The same idempotency key, so the server can recognize the repeat.
The API key again, in the prompt.
A higher temperature so the retry looks different.
A fresh order id every time, on purpose.
questions.why: Reads can retry more freely. An order cannot.

questions.case: A demo puts the API key in the browser script. The button places an order. On a timeout the client sends the same order again. The invoice shows two charges and a token spike from the retries.

questions.q: How do you explain the token spike?
choices: Count tokens in, tokens out, and the retries. The nicer prompt is not the first suspect.
Blame the font in the demo.
Assume the vendor changed the price mid-request and stop.
Delete the logs and estimate from memory.
questions.why: The bill is those counts. A spike without them is a guess.

questions.q: What should the policy have done before the paste?
choices: Asked the model whether the paste felt appropriate.
Allowed it if the email sounded kind.
Named that record as data that does not go into a prompt.
Stored the record in the weights folder for next time.
questions.why: A policy you apply after the paste is a postmortem, not a control.
questions.incidentTitle: A customer record pasted into the prompt
questions.case: A teammate pastes a customer record, including an account number, and asks the model to draft a refund email. The loop is ready to send the draft because the prose looks finished. The record is now in the request log.

questions.q: The draft is excellent. Why is send still blocked?
choices: Sending waits for a person. A finished draft is not an approval.
Because the model used a high temperature.
Because the font is wrong.
Because excellent prose is always a policy violation.
questions.why: The side effect is the send, not the writing.
questions.incidentTitle: A customer record pasted into the prompt
questions.case: A teammate pastes a customer record, including an account number, and asks the model to draft a refund email. The loop is ready to send the draft because the prose looks finished. The record is now in the request log.

questions.q: What do you do about the account number that already left?
choices: Treat it as exposed: rotate or protect what you can, and keep it out of the next retry.
Assume the vendor forgot the body.
Paste it again with a shorter prompt.
Put the number in the system prompt so it is “official.”
questions.why: Redacting the screen does not pull the log back.
questions.incidentTitle: A customer record pasted into the prompt
questions.case: A teammate pastes a customer record, including an account number, and asks the model to draft a refund email. The loop is ready to send the draft because the prose looks finished. The record is now in the request log.

questions.q: How should a later refund draft get the account facts?
choices: From the model’s memory of the last paste.
From a tool that reads the record outside the prompt, with a person on the send.
From a fine-tune on the customer table.
From a screenshot in the prompt.
questions.why: The model can draft from a minimum. The secret stays in the system that already holds it.
